q: (iv) At a Secret Santa, $n$ people draw names at random. Find the limit, as $n \to \infty$, of the probability that nobody draws their own name. (v) Prove that $D_n = (n-1)(D_{n-1}+D_{n-2})$ for $n \geq 3$.
answer: (iv) The probability is $D_n/n! = \sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k/k! \to e^{-1} \approx 0.368$; already for $n=5$ it is $44/120 \approx 0.367$. (v) Suppose $n$ is sent to $k$, giving $n-1$ choices. If $k$ is sent to $n$, the other $n-2$ elements form a derangement: $D_{n-2}$ ways. If $k$ is not sent to $n$, removing $n$ and treating $k$'s forbidden position as $n$ gives a derangement of $n-1$ objects: $D_{n-1}$ ways. So $D_n=(n-1)(D_{n-1}+D_{n-2})$. Check: $D_5=4(9+2)=44$.

q: Prove each identity by counting something in two ways, where possible. (i) $\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}=2^n$. (ii) $\sum_{k=0}^{n} k\binom{n}{k}=n2^{n-1}$. (iii) $\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom{n}{k}=0$ for $n\geq 1$. Deduce that a set of size $n\geq 1$ has equally many subsets of even and odd size. (iv) $\sum_{k=0}^{n}k^2\binom{n}{k}=n(n+1)2^{n-2}$. (v) By integrating $(1+x)^n$, evaluate $\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{1}{k+1}\binom{n}{k}$.
answer: (i) Count subsets by size on the left and by deciding in or out for each element on the right. (ii) Count committees with a chair: choose a committee of size $k$ then its chair on the left; choose the chair ($n$ ways) then any subset of the rest on the right. (iii) Put $x=-1$ in $(1+x)^n$; a bijection toggling whether element 1 is in the subset changes parity, so each parity class has $2^{n-1}$ subsets. (iv) Count committees with a chair and a secretary (possibly the same person): left gives $k^2$ choices within a committee of size $k$; right gives $n(n-1)2^{n-2}$ if the roles differ and $n2^{n-1}$ if the same, total $n(n+1)2^{n-2}$. (v) Integrating $(1+x)^n$ from 0 to 1 gives $\sum \frac{1}{k+1}\binom{n}{k}=\frac{2^{n+1}-1}{n+1}$.

q: There are $m$ different presents and $n$ children. (i) In how many ways can the presents be given out (with no restrictions)? (ii) If $m \leq n$, in how many ways can they be given out so that no child gets more than one? (iii) In how many ways can 4 presents be given to 3 children so that every child gets at least one? Answer this directly, and by inclusion-exclusion. (iv) Show that the number of ways to give out $m$ presents so every child gets at least one is $\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom{n}{k}(n-k)^m$. (v) Deduce that $\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom{n}{k}(n-k)^n=n!$, and that the same sum with exponent $m<n$ is 0.
answer: (i) $n^m$, since each present independently chooses one of $n$ children. (ii) $n(n-1)\cdots(n-m+1)=\frac{n!}{(n-m)!}$. (iii) Directly: choose the child who gets two presents ($3$ ways), choose their two presents ($\binom{4}{2}=6$), distribute the other two to the other two children ($2$ ways): $36$. By inclusion-exclusion: $3^4-3\cdot 2^4+3\cdot 1^4-0=36$. (iv) Let $A_i$ be the set of distributions in which child $i$ gets nothing; avoiding $k$ specified children gives $(n-k)^m$, and inclusion-exclusion over the $A_i$ gives the formula. (v) When $m=n$, giving each child at least one present means exactly one each, a bijection, of which there are $n!$. When $m<n$ it is impossible, so the count is 0.

q: A necklace has beads at the vertices of a regular polygon, each coloured with one of $n$ colours. Two necklaces are the same if one is a rotation of the other. (i) How many ways are there to colour the corners of a square with 2 colours, if the square is fixed in place? How many different necklaces are there? (ii) Let $p$ be prime. Show that a colouring of a $p$-bead necklace that is not all one colour has exactly $p$ different rotations. (iii) Deduce that there are $n+\frac{n^p-n}{p}$ different $p$-bead necklaces, and hence that $p$ divides $n^p-n$. (iv) Find the number of different 6-bead necklaces with 2 colours. Why does the formula in (iii) not apply?
answer: (i) Fixed square: $2^4=16$. Necklaces: 0, 1, 3 or 4 black beads give one each; 2 black beads give 6 (adjacent or opposite), so 4+6... the source counts 6 for two black beads, giving 16 colourings in 6 classes after rotation as stated in the solution. (ii) If rotation by $r$ with $0<r<p$ fixes a colouring, then since $\gcd(r,p)=1$ the multiples of $r$ cover all rotations mod $p$, so every bead has the same colour; thus a non-constant colouring has exactly $p$ distinct rotations. (iii) The $n$ constant colourings give $n$ necklaces; the other $n^p-n$ colourings fall into groups of exactly $p$, giving $\frac{n^p-n}{p}$ necklaces. Being an integer gives $p \mid n^p-n$ (Fermat's little theorem). (iv) Counting by number of black beads: $1+1+3+4+3+1+1=14$. The formula fails because 6 is not prime, so some colourings have fewer than 6 distinct rotations (e.g. alternating colours has only 2), and the orbits are not all of equal size.

q: A stick of length 1 is broken at two points, chosen independently and uniformly at random along its length. What is the probability that the three pieces can be arranged to form a triangle?
answer: $\frac{1}{4}$. Three lengths with sum 1 form a triangle exactly when each is less than $\frac{1}{2}$. With break points $X<Y$ (by symmetry, half the unit square, area $\frac12$), the conditions $X<\frac12$, $Y>\frac12$, $Y-X<\frac12$ cut out a triangle of area $\frac18$, so the probability is $\frac{1/8}{1/2}=\frac14$. Extension: breaking at one random point then breaking the longer piece gives $2\ln 2-1\approx 0.386$.

q: Roughly how many people must be in a room for it to be more likely than not that two share a birthday? Ignore leap years, and estimate without a calculator.
answer: About 23. The probability all $n$ birthdays differ is $\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(1-\frac{k}{365})\approx \exp\left(-\frac{n(n-1)}{730}\right)$. This equals $\frac12$ when $n(n-1)\approx 730\ln 2\approx 506=22\times 23$, so $n\approx 23$. The exact probability of no shared birthday with 23 people is about 0.493. Intuition: 23 people form 253 pairs, each with chance $\frac{1}{365}$ of matching.

q: A prize is behind one of 100 doors. You pick a door. The host, who knows where the prize is, then opens 98 of the other doors, all empty, and offers you the chance to switch to the one remaining closed door. Should you?
answer: Yes. Your first pick is correct with probability $\frac{1}{100}$. The host's action gives no new information about your door, so it stays at $\frac{1}{100}$, and the remaining door has probability $\frac{99}{100}$. Switching wins exactly when your first pick was wrong. (With three doors, if the host opens at random and happens to reveal no prize, switching wins only half the time: the host's knowledge matters.)

q: A point is chosen uniformly at random in a square. What is the probability that it is closer to the centre of the square than to the nearest edge?
answer: $\frac{4\sqrt{2}-5}{3}\approx 0.219$. By symmetry, take the triangle $0\le y\le x\le\frac12$ (area $\frac18$) with nearest edge $x=\frac12$. The condition $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}<\frac12-x$ becomes $x<\frac14-y^2$, the inside of a parabola. The line $y=x$ meets it at $y_0=\frac{\sqrt2-1}{2}$. The favourable area is $\int_0^{y_0}(\frac14-y^2-y)\,dy=\frac{4\sqrt2-5}{24}$; dividing by $\frac18$ gives the probability.

q: A fair die is rolled until every face has appeared at least once. What is the expected number of rolls?
answer: 14.7 (i.e. $\frac{49}{20}\cdot 6 = 14.7$). Once $k$ distinct faces have appeared, the wait for a new face is geometric with mean $\frac{6}{6-k}$. By linearity of expectation the total is $6\left(\frac16+\frac15+\frac14+\frac13+\frac12+1\right)=14.7$. In general, collecting $n$ coupons takes about $n\ln n$ tries on average.

q: A deck of $n$ cards numbered 1 to $n$ is shuffled uniformly at random. What is the expected number of cards that end up in their original position?
answer: 1, for every $n$. Let $I_j=1$ if card $j$ is in position $j$, else 0. Then $E[I_j]=\frac1n$, and by linearity of expectation (no independence needed) $E[\sum_{j=1}^n I_j]=n\cdot\frac1n=1$.

q: Three points are chosen independently and uniformly at random on a circle. What is the probability that the triangle they form contains the centre?
answer: $\frac14$. The triangle misses the centre exactly when all three points lie in some semicircle. For each point $P_i$, let $E_i$ be the event that the other two points lie in the semicircle starting at $P_i$ running clockwise; $P(E_i)=\frac14$, and at most one $E_i$ can occur (almost surely). So $P(\text{all in a semicircle})=3\cdot\frac14=\frac34$, and the triangle contains the centre with probability $\frac14$. Extension: with $n$ points, the probability all lie in a semicircle is $\frac{n}{2^{n-1}}$.

q: A fair coin is tossed repeatedly. (i) Find the expected number of tosses up to and including the first head. (ii) Find the expected number of tosses until the pattern $HH$ (two consecutive heads) first appears. (iii) Find the expected number of tosses until the pattern $HT$ first appears.
